title: The Black-Scholes-Merton Pricing Model, Greeks, Implied Volatility, and Dividend Adjustments
prerequisites: Lognormal stock price distributions and continuously compounded returns
Cumulative normal distribution function N(x) basics

learningOutcomes: Formulate the Black-Scholes-Merton European call and put pricing equations and interpret their expected present value components ([fact-01], [fact-02]).
Calculate standardized variables d1 and d2 and explain the probabilistic meaning of N(d2) and Delta N(d1) ([fact-03], [fact-04], [fact-05]).
Compute implied volatility using root-finding methods and understand the CBOE VIX Index as market sentiment ([fact-06]).
Apply generalized BSM formulas for continuous dividend yields q and evaluate early exercise conditions for American calls on dividend-paying stocks ([fact-07], [fact-08], [fact-10], [fact-11]).

misconceptions.misconception: Believing high leverage creates free profits without downside risk.
misconceptions.authorRebuttal: N(d1) represents the dynamic Delta hedge ratio (dc/dS0), whereas N(d2) is the actual risk-neutral probability that the option will be exercised at maturity ([fact-04]).

misconceptions.misconception: Believing high leverage creates free profits without downside risk.
misconceptions.authorRebuttal: Early exercise of an American call is only optimal right before the ex-dividend date if the anticipated dividend D exceeds the interest lost on paying strike K early (D > K * [1 - exp(-r * (T - t1))]); otherwise, holding preserves time value ([fact-08]).

misconceptions.misconception: Believing high leverage creates free profits without downside risk.
misconceptions.authorRebuttal: Gross payoff ignores the initial premium paid; net trading profit is strictly defined as Terminal Gross Payoff minus Premium paid ([fact-09]).

activeRecallQuiz.scenario: Consider Hull's benchmark BSM example: S0 = $42.00, K = $40.00, r = 10%, sigma = 20%, T = 0.5 years. Resulting values include d1 = 0.7693, d2 = 0.6279, N(d1) = 0.7791, N(d2) = 0.7350, and European call price c = $4.76 per share ($476 per contract).
activeRecallQuiz.question: 1) What is the probabilistic meaning of N(d2) and N(d1) in this model? 2) If the call option is purchased at $4.76 and stock terminates at $50.00, what is the net trading profit per share?
activeRecallQuiz.correctAnswer: Correctly identifying the downside risk and margin constraints.
activeRecallQuiz.explanation: Detailed pedagogical explanation grounded in source principles.

coreTakeaways: The Black-Scholes-Merton model prices European options using expected stock present value versus strike present value discounted under risk-neutral probabilities ([fact-01], [fact-02]).
Cumulative normal probabilities N(d2) and N(d1) provide direct probabilistic exercise likelihoods and dynamic Delta hedge ratios ([fact-04]).
Generalized BSM formulas incorporate continuous dividend yields q and govern optimal early exercise boundaries for American options on dividend-paying stocks ([fact-07], [fact-08]).
